CHAPTER 1



Data Communication Fundamentals


1.1 Data, Information and Data Communication


Data is raw, unprocessed facts. The number 85, the word Dhaka, a photograph — on their own
these mean nothing.
Information is processed data — data that has been given meaning. “85 marks in Mathematics” is
information.
Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through some transmission
medium such as a copper wire, a fibre-optic cable or radio waves.
  Four Characteristics of a Good Data Communication System

  Remember these four. They are asked as a direct one-mark definition question.
  • Delivery — data must reach the correct destination, and only that destination.
  • Accuracy — data must arrive unaltered. Corrupted data is unusable.
  • Timeliness — data must arrive on time. Late video or voice data is useless (this is called
    real-time transmission).
  • Jitter — the variation in packet arrival time. If packets arrive at 20 ms, then 40 ms, then
    25 ms, the audio or video will sound or look uneven.

  Easy Way to Remember

  D-A-T-J — Delivery, Accuracy, Timeliness, Jitter. Think of it as “DATa Jitter”.


1.2 Five Components of Data Communication



                                                  Message




                       Sender            Transmission Medium                 Receiver


                                      Protocol governs the entire exchange


1. Message — the information to be communicated: text, numbers, pictures, audio, video.
2. Sender — the device that sends the message: computer, workstation, telephone handset, video
   camera.
3. Receiver — the device that receives the message: computer, workstation, telephone, television.
4. Transmission medium — the physical path: twisted pair, coaxial cable, fibre-optic cable, radio
   waves.
5. Protocol — a set of agreed rules governing the communication. Without a shared protocol, two
   connected devices still cannot understand each other.

1.3 Data Flow: Simplex, Half-Duplex, Full-Duplex



   Asked In

   Differentiate between half-duplex and full-duplex transmission. — BPSC AP 2023
   What is data communication? Define simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex. — ICT Ministry AP
   2017, BKKB AP 2017
   How many modes are used in data transfer through networks? Explain briefly. — Combined Bank
   SO(IT) 2024

1.3.1 Simplex

Communication is one-directional only. One device only sends; the other only receives. The entire
capacity of the channel is used by the sending device.
Examples: keyboard to computer, computer to monitor, radio broadcast, television broadcast.

1.3.2 Half-Duplex

Both devices can send and receive, but not at the same time. When one is sending, the other must
wait. The whole channel capacity is taken over by whichever device is currently transmitting.
Examples: walkie-talkie, CB radio, traditional Ethernet with a hub.

1.3.3 Full-Duplex

Both devices can send and receive simultaneously. The channel capacity is shared between the two
directions — either by using two separate physical paths, or by dividing the bandwidth in two.
Examples: telephone conversation, mobile phone call, modern Ethernet with a switch.

                            Half-Duplex    Station A                                 Station B

                                                           one direction at a time



                            Full-Duplex    Station A                                 Station B

                                                           both directions at once

1.4 Serial and Parallel Transmission


1.4.1 Parallel Transmission

Multiple bits (usually 8) are sent at the same time over n separate wires.
Advantage: fast — n times the speed of serial for the same clock rate.
Disadvantages: expensive (needs n wires), and only practical over short distances because of skew
(bits arriving at slightly different times) and crosstalk.

1.4.2 Serial Transmission

Bits are sent one after another over a single wire.
Advantage: cheap, works over long distances.
Disadvantage: slower per clock cycle — but modern serial links run at such high clock rates that
they now beat parallel in practice (USB, SATA, PCIe are all serial).
   Common Mistake

   Many candidates write “parallel is always faster”. This was true historically but is wrong today.
   Parallel suffers from clock skew at high speeds, which is exactly why USB and SATA replaced
   the old parallel port and IDE cable. Write both the theory and this modern qualification for full
   marks.


1.5 Synchronous, Asynchronous and Isochronous Transmission



   Asked In

   Distinguish between synchronous and asynchronous transmission. — RAKUB ANSE 2023

1.5.1 Asynchronous Transmission

Data is sent one character (byte) at a time. Each byte is wrapped with a start bit (0) at the
beginning and one or two stop bits (1) at the end. Between bytes there may be a gap of any length
(idle time).
There is no shared clock. The receiver re-synchronises at every start bit.
Overhead: for 8 data bits you send at least 10 bits — a 20% overhead.

1.5.2 Synchronous Transmission

Data is sent as a continuous stream of bits with no start bits, no stop bits and no gaps. The bits are
grouped into frames. Sender and receiver share timing, either through a common clock line or by
extracting the clock from the data itself (self-synchronising line codes such as Manchester encoding).

1.5.3 Isochronous Transmission

Guarantees that data arrives at a fixed rate with fixed delay — essential for real-time audio and
video, where an uneven arrival rate (jitter) ruins playback.

Analog signal — a continuously varying wave. It has infinitely many values in its range. Human
voice, temperature and the old telephone line are analog.
Digital signal — discrete steps, usually just two levels representing 0 and 1. It looks like a square

2.2 Bandwidth, Bit Rate, Baud Rate and Throughput


2.2.1 Bandwidth

Bandwidth has two different meanings and the exam tests whether you know both.
Bandwidth in hertz — the range of frequencies a channel can carry. If a line passes frequencies from
1000 Hz to 5000 Hz, its bandwidth is 5000 − 1000 = 4000 Hz.
Bandwidth in bits per second — the number of bits a channel can carry per second.

2.2.2 Bit Rate vs Baud Rate

Bit rate = number of bits sent per second (bps).
Baud rate (signal rate) = number of signal units / symbols sent per second (baud).

2.3 Transmission Impairments


Signals travel through imperfect media, so the signal that arrives is not the signal that was sent.
Three impairments are asked about.

2.3.1 Attenuation

Loss of signal strength (energy) as the signal travels through the medium. Longer distance means
weaker signal. The remedy is an amplifier (for analog) or a repeater (for digital).
Attenuation is measured in decibels (dB):

where P1 is the input power and P2 the output power.

A negative dB value means the signal was attenuated (lost power). A positive value means it was
amplified.

   Example 2.6 — Cascaded dB

  A signal passes through three points. From point 1 to 2 it loses 3 dB, from 2 to 3 it is amplified

2.3.2 Distortion

The signal changes its shape. This happens in composite signals, where different frequency compo-
nents travel at different speeds through the medium and therefore arrive with different delays. The
received wave no longer looks like the transmitted wave.

2.3.3 Noise

Unwanted signals added to the original. Types:
• Thermal noise — random motion of electrons in the wire.
• Induced noise — from motors, appliances and other electrical machinery.
• Crosstalk — signal from one wire leaking into an adjacent wire (you hear another conversation
  on the phone).
• Impulse noise — a sudden high-energy spike, e.g. from lightning or a power surge.
Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) measures how much stronger the signal is than the noise:

A high SNR is good. A low SNR means the signal is buried in noise.

CHAPTER 3



Digital and Analog Transmission


3.1 Line Coding



  Asked In

  What is line coding? What are the different line coding techniques? — SPCBL AME 2021

Line coding is the process of converting digital data into a digital signal. The sender encodes bits
into a signal; the receiver decodes the signal back into bits.

3.1.1 Characteristics of a Good Line Code

• Self-synchronisation — the receiver can recover the clock from the signal itself, so it never drifts
  out of step.
• No DC component — the average voltage should be zero, so the signal can pass through trans-
  formers and long cables.
• Low bandwidth requirement and built-in error detection are also desirable.

3.1.2 Categories of Line Coding

     Category          Schemes                      How It Works

     Unipolar          NRZ                          One non-zero voltage level; 0 is zero volts. Has a
                                                    strong DC component.
     Polar             NRZ-L, NRZ-I, RZ, Manch-     Uses both positive and negative voltages.
                       ester, Differential Manch-
                       ester
     Bipolar           AMI, Pseudoternary           Three levels: positive, zero, negative.
     Multilevel        2B1Q, 8B6T, 4D-PAM5          Encodes m data bits into n signal elements.
     Multitransition   MLT-3                        Transition-based, reduces required bandwidth.



3.1.3 The Schemes You Must Be Able to Draw

NRZ-L (Non-Return-to-Zero, Level) — the voltage level determines the bit. Typically 0 = positive
voltage, 1 = negative voltage.
NRZ-I (Non-Return-to-Zero, Invert) — the presence of a transition at the start of the bit period
means 1; no transition means 0.
RZ (Return-to-Zero) — uses three values. The signal returns to zero in the middle of every bit. Good
synchronisation, but needs double the bandwidth.
Manchester — combines RZ and NRZ-L. There is always a transition in the middle of every bit. Low-
to-high = 1, high-to-low = 0 (IEEE convention). Self-synchronising, no DC component — this is why
classic 10 Mbps Ethernet used it.
Differential Manchester — always a mid-bit transition for synchronisation, and the bit value is
decided by whether there is also a transition at the start of the bit: transition at start = 0, no

3.2 Block Coding and Scrambling


Block coding converts a block of m bits into a block of n bits, where n > m. It is written as mB/nB.
The extra bits provide redundancy for synchronisation and error detection.
Examples: 4B/5B (used in 100BaseTX Fast Ethernet), 8B/10B (Gigabit Ethernet), 8B/6T.
Scrambling replaces long sequences of zeros with a special pattern so that synchronisation is not
lost. Two schemes: B8ZS (used in North America) and HDB3 (used in Europe and Japan).

3.3 Pulse Code Modulation (PCM)



   Asked In

   What is modulation? Describe the pulse code modulation (PCM) technique. — BPSC AE 2022

PCM converts an analog signal into digital data. It is what happens inside every digital telephone
system and every audio recording. There are three steps.

                              1. Sampling                                     3. Encoding
             Analog                                 2. Quantization                               Digital
                                 (PAM)                                         (to binary)



1. Sampling — measure the amplitude of the analog signal at regular intervals. The result is a series
   of pulses (Pulse Amplitude Modulation, PAM).
2. Quantization — round each sampled amplitude to the nearest of a fixed set of levels. This step
   introduces a small permanent error called quantization noise.
3. Encoding — convert each quantized level into a binary code.

5.1.1 Circuit Switching

A dedicated physical path is established between sender and receiver before any data flows, and it
stays reserved for the whole session. The classic example is the old telephone network.
Three phases: setup → data transfer → teardown.
Advantages: guaranteed bandwidth, constant and predictable delay, no packet ordering problem,
ideal for continuous voice.
Disadvantages: the path is reserved even when idle (very wasteful for bursty computer data), long
setup time, and if the path breaks the whole call drops.

5.1.2 Packet Switching

Data is broken into packets, each carrying a header with source and destination addresses. Packets
are forwarded hop by hop and share links with everybody else’s traffic. No dedicated path is reserved.

• Datagram approach (connectionless) — each packet is routed independently and may take a
  different path. Packets can arrive out of order or be lost. This is how IP works.
• Virtual circuit approach (connection-oriented) — a logical path is set up first and all packets
  follow it in order, but the link is still shared. Used by Frame Relay and ATM.

5.1.3 Message Switching

The whole message is sent to an intermediate node, stored completely, then forwarded when a link
is free (store-and-forward). No length limit on messages, but delay is very high. Now obsolete
except in email-style systems.

   Computer traffic is bursty — a short download, then a long silence. Circuit switching would

Error Detection, Correction and Flow Control


7.1 Types of Error


Single-bit error — exactly one bit in the data unit changes from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0. Rare in serial
transmission.
Burst error — two or more bits in the data unit change. The burst length is counted from the first
corrupted bit to the last, and bits in between may be unaffected. This is the common case, because
noise usually lasts longer than one bit period.
  Easy Way to Remember

  The faster the data rate, the more bits fit inside the same burst of noise. A 1 ms noise spike
  corrupts 10 bits at 10 kbps, but 1,000 bits at 1 Mbps. This is why high-speed links need strong
  error control.


7.2 Redundancy


All error detection works the same way: the sender adds extra bits (redundant bits) computed from
the data. The receiver recomputes them and compares. If they disagree, an error occurred.

7.3 Parity Check


7.3.1 Simple Parity Check

One parity bit is added so that the total number of 1s becomes even (even parity) or odd (odd
parity).
  Example 7.1 — Even Parity

  Data to send: 1011001
  Count the 1s: 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 4 ones. That is already even, so the parity bit is 0.
  Transmitted: 10110010
  Now take data 1010001. Number of 1s = 3 (odd), so the parity bit must be 1 to make it even.
  Transmitted: 10100011

  Common Mistake

  Simple parity detects all odd numbers of bit errors but cannot detect an even number of
  errors. If two bits flip, the parity is unchanged and the error passes undetected. It also cannot
  correct anything.

7.3.2 Two-Dimensional Parity Check

Data is arranged in a table of rows and columns. A parity bit is computed for every row and every
column. This detects most burst errors and can correct a single-bit error (because the wrong row and
wrong column intersect at the faulty bit).

7.4 Checksum


Used by TCP, UDP and IP. It works on blocks of n bits.
   Checksum Procedure

   At the sender:     (1) divide the data into k blocks of n bits; (2) add all blocks using one’s
   complement arithmetic; (3) complement the sum — this is the checksum; (4) send data +
   checksum.
   At the receiver: (1) add all received blocks including the checksum; (2) complement the
   result; (3) if the result is all zeros, the data is accepted; otherwise it is discarded.

   Example 7.2 — Checksum with 4-bit Blocks

   Data blocks: 1001, 1110, 0011
   Sender side:

                                                 1001 + 1110 = 10111 (5 bits — carry out)
                            wrap the carry: 0111 + 1 = 1000
                                                 1000 + 0011 = 1011 (no carry)

   Sum = 1011. Complement it: Checksum = 0100.
   Transmitted: 1001 1110 0011 0100
   Receiver side (no error):

                                               1001 + 1110 + 0011 + 0100 = 1111

   Complement of 1111 is 0000 → all zeros → data accepted.


7.5 Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC)


The most powerful and most widely used detection method — Ethernet, Wi-Fi and almost every link
layer uses it. It is based on binary division using XOR (modulo-2 arithmetic, no borrows or carries).
   CRC Procedure

   Sender: (1) the divisor (generator polynomial) has n bits; (2) append n − 1 zeros to the
   data; (3) divide by the generator using XOR; (4) the remainder (n − 1 bits) is the CRC;
   (5) replace the appended zeros with the CRC and transmit.
   Receiver: divide the whole received bit string by the same generator.
   Remainder = 0 → no error. Remainder ̸= 0 → error, discard the frame.

Each parity bit checks the positions whose binary representation has a 1 in the corresponding place:
• P1 (position 1) checks positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 — check 1, skip 1
• P2 (position 2) checks positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11 — check 2, skip 2
• P4 (position 4) checks positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15 — check 4, skip 4
• P8 (position 8) checks positions 8–15 — check 8, skip 8

   The codeword 0110011 was sent, but 0110111 was received (bit 5 flipped).

   C2 (positions 2,3,6,7) = 1, 1, 1, 1 → four 1s, even → passes → C2 = 0
   C4 (positions 4,5,6,7) = 0, 1, 1, 1 → three 1s, odd → fails → C4 = 1
   Form the syndrome as C4 C2 C1 = 1012 = 5

7.7 Flow Control and Error Control Protocols


Flow control stops a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. Error control is flow control
plus retransmission of damaged or lost frames — this is called ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest).

7.7.1 Stop-and-Wait ARQ

Send one frame, then wait for its acknowledgement before sending the next. A timer runs; if the
ACK does not arrive before it expires, the frame is retransmitted.
Simple, but very inefficient on long or fast links, because the sender is idle for one full round-trip
time after every single frame.

7.7.2 Go-Back-N ARQ

The sender may transmit up to N frames (the window) without waiting. If frame k is damaged, the
receiver discards it and every frame after it, and the sender retransmits frame k onwards.
Window size: 2m − 1 where m is the number of bits in the sequence number.

7.7.3 Selective Repeat ARQ

Only the specific damaged frame is retransmitted. The receiver buffers out-of-order frames and
reorders them. More efficient in bandwidth but needs more memory and more complex logic.
Window size: 2m−1 .

8.1 Multiple Access Protocols


When many devices share one medium, something must decide who transmits when — otherwise
signals collide.

8.1.1 ALOHA

Pure ALOHA — transmit whenever you have data. If a collision occurs, wait a random time and
retry. Maximum efficiency only 18.4%.
Slotted ALOHA — time is divided into slots and stations may transmit only at the start of a slot. This
halves the vulnerable period, doubling efficiency to 36.8%.

8.1.2 CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access)

“Listen before you talk.” A station senses the channel first and transmits only if it is idle.
Persistence methods:
• 1-persistent — if idle, send immediately (probability 1). High collision chance.
• Non-persistent — if busy, wait a random time, then sense again. Fewer collisions but longer
  delay.
• p-persistent — used with slotted channels; if idle, send with probability p.

8.1.3 CSMA/CD — Collision Detection

“Listen before and while you talk.” Used in wired Ethernet. If a collision is detected during trans-
mission, the station immediately stops, sends a jam signal, and waits a random period determined
by the binary exponential backoff algorithm before retrying.

8.1.4 CSMA/CA — Collision Avoidance

Used in wireless (Wi-Fi, 802.11). In wireless a station cannot listen while transmitting (its own
signal drowns everything else), so collisions cannot be detected — they must be avoided. It uses
interframe spacing, a contention window with random backoff, and explicit ACKs. Optionally it uses
RTS/CTS handshaking to solve the hidden terminal problem.

10.3.1 Distance Vector Routing

Each router tells its direct neighbours everything it knows about the whole network (“routing by
rumour”). It uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm and the metric is usually hop count.
Updates are sent periodically (RIP: every 30 seconds) to neighbours only.
Problem: count-to-infinity. When a network goes down, bad information circulates and hop counts
climb slowly. Remedies: split horizon, poison reverse, hold-down timers, and defining infinity as
16.
Protocols: RIP, RIPv2, IGRP, EIGRP (advanced/hybrid).

10.3.2 Link State Routing

Each router discovers its own directly connected links, then floods that information to every router in
the area. Every router therefore builds an identical complete map of the topology and independently
runs Dijkstra’s shortest path first algorithm on it.
Updates are event-triggered — sent only when something changes.
Protocols: OSPF, IS-IS.

13.3 Hashing and Digital Signatures


A hash function (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) produces a fixed-length digest from any input. It is one-
way — you cannot reverse it — and any change to the input completely changes the digest. Used for
password storage and integrity checking.
A digital signature is the hash of a message, encrypted with the sender’s private key. It provides
authentication, integrity and non-repudiation all at once.
A digital certificate binds a public key to an identity and is issued by a trusted Certificate Authority
(CA). This is the basis of PKI (Public Key Infrastructure).

13.4 Firewalls and VPN


A firewall filters traffic between networks according to rules.
• Packet filtering — inspects IP addresses, ports and protocol; stateless.
• Stateful inspection — tracks the state of connections; far more effective.
• Application / proxy firewall — understands the application protocol itself.
• Next-generation firewall — adds intrusion prevention and deep packet inspection.
A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel across the public Internet, so a remote
branch or employee can safely reach the internal network. Protocols: IPsec, SSL/TLS VPN, L2TP,
PPTP (obsolete and insecure).
DMZ (Demilitarised Zone) — an isolated network segment holding public-facing servers (web,
mail), separated by firewalls from the internal network, so that a breach of a public server does not
expose internal systems.

   Written Exam Technique

   1. Start every answer with a one-sentence definition, even for comparison questions.
   2. Use tables for every “differentiate” or “distinguish” question — they are faster to write and
   easier for the examiner to award marks from.
   3. Draw the diagram whenever one exists. Diagrams carry independent marks.
   4. For numericals, show every step. Method marks survive an arithmetic slip.
   5. Give a Bangladeshi or everyday example where you can — it shows understanding rather
   than memorisation.
   6. Manage time: roughly 1.5 minutes per mark. Do not spend fifteen minutes perfecting a
   five-mark answer.
